answer.label: Not Salvador Dalí — a modern saying he never said
answer.authorDates: Earliest named source (Reader’s Digest, 1997) · biography undocumented
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Salvador Dalí ever said or wrote this. A near-variant simile — “intelligence without ambition is like a bird without wings” — appeared anonymously in 1996; the exact modern wording (“is a bird without wings”) is first seen in 1997, credited to C. Archie Danielson in Reader’s Digest Quotable Quotes. The Dalí label only shows up around 2004, most likely from an alphabetical mix-up between “Danielson” and “Dalí,” per Quote Investigator ↗.

source.excerpt: Intelligence without ambition is a bird without wings.
trail: 1908: Walter H. Cottingham writes a close precursor in System: The Magazine of Business — “A man without ambition is like a bird without wings” — about ambition, not intelligence, per Quote Investigator ↗.

1996: a near-variant simile — “intelligence without ambition is like a bird without wings” — appears anonymously; the exact modern wording (“is a bird without wings”) is first seen in 1997, credited to C. Archie Danielson in Reader’s Digest Quotable Quotes ↗.
c. 2004: a newspaper reassigns the line to Salvador Dalí; Quote Investigator finds no substantive evidence ↗ for the Dalí attribution and blames an alphabetical “Danielson/Dalí” mix-up.
source.excerptNote: The line circulates over Salvador Dalí’s name, but it is absent from his documented works; the earliest match is an anonymous 1996 simile variant (“like a bird without wings”), and the exact modern wording is first credited to Danielson in 1997.
source.rightsNote: The exact wording is a modern aphorism of uncertain authorship — a simile variant appeared anonymously in 1996, and the exact wording was first credited to C. Archie Danielson in 1997 — with no identifiable pre-1931 source, so no public-domain status can be asserted. It is not drawn from any dated work by Salvador Dalí. The 1908 Cottingham precursor is a different sentence, not this line.

author.name: C. Archie Danielson
author.heading: About C. Archie Danielson
author.metaLine: Earliest named source of the modern wording · Reader's Digest Quotable Quotes, 1997
author.bio: C. Archie Danielson is the name on the earliest named printing of the exact modern wording, in Reader’s Digest Quotable Quotes (1997) — but virtually nothing is documented about the person, and an anonymous simile variant (“like a bird without wings”) predates it by a year (1996), so even this credit is uncertain. The clearest documented ancestor of the thought is a 1908 line by Sherwin-Williams executive Walter H. Cottingham (1866–1930), then vice-president and general manager and later the company’s president: “A man without ambition is like a bird without wings” — about ambition, with no mention of intelligence. Salvador Dalí, who died in 1989, is not linked to the saying in any of his own writings or interviews.
